title: a canon write reports ok and is silently lost as the third of three rapid calls
body:
**A CANON WRITE REPORTS `ok: ... created` AND IS SILENTLY LOST WHEN IT FOLLOWS TWO OTHERS IN QUICK SUCCESSION.**

**TWO INDEPENDENT INSTANCES, TWO DIFFERENT VERBS, SAME POSITION.** vc lost `AC-17.17` as the third of three rapid `ac new` calls in one shell invocation; ic lost `AT-00.7` as the third of three rapid `at new` calls in one shell invocation. Both printed `ok: ... created`. Both were absent afterwards from the extract, from `acceptance.md`, and from `ac list` / `at list`. **Both landed and verified when the identical call was re-run alone minutes later.**

The loss is silent in the worst direction: the verb's own success line is the only report, and it is wrong. **A commit message then carries the belief forward** -- `222e5d57` says *mint AC-17.15/16/17* and has never contained 17.17 -- so three boards believed a row existed.

**HYPOTHESIS, MECHANISM-LEVEL, NOT YET DRIVEN TO A DELIBERATE REPRODUCTION.** `ac new` / `at new` write the store and re-render `acceptance.md`. `intentd` registers a project and watches it -- `registry.rs`: *a project the daemon is answering for is a project the daemon is watching*, and the watch wraps a **debouncer**. The watcher treats the render as an external edit and ingests it back into the store. On rapid successive calls the debounced ingest of render N can land after write N+1, overwriting it. A debouncer collapsing three rapid renders into one late ingest is exactly the shape that loses the last write and no other.

**EVIDENCE FOR, AND ITS LIMIT STATED.** In a freshly created scratch project outside the live tree, **18 rapid `ac new` calls across six trials of three lost nothing** -- 3 of 3 every time. The two real losses are both in this project, which the daemon has served all day and therefore watches. **WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: that the scratch project was unregistered.** `daemon status` answers from both locations and does not itself register anything, and the calls in both trees ran in-process rather than through `--daemon`, so the in-process path is not the discriminator. The registration state of the scratch tree was not measured, so the two arms differ in a way that is strongly suggested and not isolated.

**WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT:** drive three rapid writes against a project whose registration state is known in both directions, and read the daemon's ingest counter (`registry.rs` exposes `ingested()`) either side of the burst.

**MITIGATION IN USE NOW, AND IT IS NOT A FIX:** one canon write at a time, then verify the artefact -- the extract and the rendered doc -- never the tool's `ok` line. Both nodes adopted it after their own instance. **A discipline is the wrong shape of answer for a write that reports success and does not happen.**
